title: Lesson 68: Disaster Recovery: Backup, Restore, RTO, RPO, and Drills
description: What recovery actually means for a Salesforce org: the difference between backup and restore, how RTO and RPO turn fuzzy promises into measurable targets, which native tools get there, and why a backup you have never restored is a backup you do not have.

questions.question: A business asks for fast recovery from an outage. What must be defined to turn that wish into a testable target?
options: A single org-wide uptime percentage applied uniformly to every capability, signed off once by IT and never revisited.
The name of the backup vendor and the exact terms of its annual support agreement and escalation contacts.
A recovery time objective and a recovery point objective set per business capability and approved by stakeholders.
A confirmation that platform-level redundancy removes any need for a customer-side recovery target.
questions.explanation: Recovery targets must be measurable and set per capability, because a revenue-critical flow and historical reporting do not warrant the same time to recover or the same tolerance for data loss.

questions.question: A client wants near-zero data loss on financial records but currently only takes daily backups. What is required beyond the daily backup?
options: Nothing more at all, because a daily backup already achieves near-zero data loss for financial records on its own without any extra tooling.
A replication mechanism such as asynchronous event streaming or change data capture, because daily backups cap data loss at a day.
A longer backup retention period, because keeping many older copies on hand reduces the amount of data lost in an outage.
A written service level agreement with the vendor that contractually waives any data loss during an outage.
questions.explanation: A daily backup can never produce a sub-day recovery point, so a near-zero objective on financial records demands a replication mechanism such as event streaming or change data capture, not simply more frequent copies.

questions.question: What does running a restore drill actually establish that an untested backup cannot?
options: That the backup can be restored within the target recovery time and loses no more than the allowed data, proven by a timed test.
That the backup files exist, are complete, and are stored in a separate location from the source data, safely out of reach of the primary org.
That the platform's infrastructure-level failover between data centers is functioning exactly as the vendor designed it.
That the recovery runbook has been written, reviewed, and formally approved by the business stakeholders before any incident.
questions.explanation: A backup is only as real as the restore you have performed; a drill times the actual recovery against the RTO and measures the data lost against the RPO, exposing the gap between the plan and reality while the stakes are a sandbox.
